query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Mo content to x = 1 in the CoCrFeNi-based composite will promote robust high-temperature oxide/molybdate glaze formation and Mo-induced σ phase strengthening that reduces wear and maintains low friction across the full temperature range, overcoming the baseline’s performance limitations.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniformly ball-milled powder mixtures containing 67.5 wt.% CoCrFeNiMox (with x = 0.2 as baseline, and variants at x = 0.5 and x = 1), 12.5 wt.% Ni-coated MoS2, 15 wt.% Ag, and 5 wt.% Cr2O3; sintered using spark plasma sintering under vacuum and 40 MPa.
generation.intervention: Increasing the Mo content to the highest studied level (x = 1) in the composite.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding ball-on-disk tests in air performed over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, using a 6 mm Si3N4 ball under an 8 N load, 0.15 m/s sliding speed, 270 m sliding distance, with SPS processing (heating to 1250 °C at 150 °C/min, 3 min hold, and furnace cooling under 40 MPa).
generation.structural_mediator: Higher Mo content induces significant FCC lattice distortion and promotes the formation of a hard, Mo-rich tetragonal σ phase. At high temperature, oxidation and tribochemical reactions result in a continuous glaze composed of silver molybdates (e.g., Ag2MoO4, Ag2Mo4O13) and NiO, which forms at the wear interface.
generation.mechanism: The dissolved Mo enhances solid-solution strengthening and the σ phase contributes second-phase strengthening to resist plastic deformation and scratching. At lower temperatures, the presence of MoS2 and Ag facilitates low-shear lubrication, while at higher temperatures the formation of a dense oxide/molybdate glaze decreases interfacial shear stresses and material removal.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Mo0.2 baseline, the Mo1 composite is expected to exhibit increased hardness and wear resistance across the full temperature range, with particularly effective glaze formation at 800 °C that yields lower wear rates and maintains comparably low friction coefficients. However, friction reduction at the intermediate temperatures (200–400 °C) may be less pronounced due to competing effects from thermal softening and lubricant film continuity.
generation.baseline: The Mo0.2 composite, which primarily forms an FCC solid solution with little σ phase, shows a friction coefficient of ~0.66 at room temperature, peaking at ~0.75 at 200 °C, then dropping to ~0.21 at 800 °C, and has wear rates that increase to a maximum at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 98.1 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m at 400 °C) before decreasing at 800 °C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under dry sliding conditions in air against a Si3N4 counterface, tested from room temperature to 800 °C under an 8 N load, 0.15 m/s sliding speed, and 270 m sliding distance. Results may differ in other environments or under different loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While increased Mo is expected to improve wear resistance and promote glaze formation at high temperatures, the exact magnitude of friction reduction at intermediate temperatures (200–400 °C) is less certain due to competing processes of lubricant layer formation and thermal softening. Environmental variations outside air are also not addressed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare composites with Mo contents of x = 0.2, 0.5, and 1 using the described SPS process. Perform ball-on-disk tribological tests across the temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) under the specified conditions. Characterize phase constitution with XRD, observe microstructure and wear tracks via SEM/EDS, measure hardness (Vickers) and compression properties, and identify tribofilm constituents (via Raman spectroscopy) on the wear surfaces.
measurements: XRD peak shifts and identification of σ-phase peaks
SEM/EDS mapping of matrix and wear track morphology
Vickers hardness and compression stress–strain tests
Profilometry to determine wear-scar dimensions and wear rates
Raman spectroscopy to confirm formation and continuity of the Mo1 high-temperature glaze
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo1 composite does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in wear resistance (i.e., lower wear rates across the test temperatures) and fails to form a coherent high-temperature oxide/molybdate glaze—resulting in similar or worse friction coefficients compared to the Mo0.2 baseline—the hypothesis will be rejected.
